WAGE CLAIM WITH THE CALIFORNIA LABOR COMMISSIONER (BERMAN HEARING) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Morgan T. Ellis · Acme Manufacturing, Inc.

INFORMATION AND BACKGROUND — DLSE WAGE CLAIM (BERMAN HEARING)
I, Morgan T. Ellis, am completing this information sheet in connection with wages I believe Acme Manufacturing, Inc. owes me. The wages at issue are described here as: Unpaid overtime for hours worked over 8 per day, in an amount currently identified as approximately ,200.00. My employment with Acme Manufacturing, Inc. is described here, where applicable, as having ended on March 14, 2026.

This information sheet describes the administrative process for filing an unpaid-wage claim with California's Division of Labor Standards Enforcement (DLSE), within the Labor Commissioner's Office — a process commonly referred to as a "Berman hearing." That process is distinct from sending a private demand letter directly to an employer, and distinct from filing a lawsuit in court.

This information sheet is not a DLSE wage claim form, is not itself filed with any agency by completing it, and does not initiate a DLSE claim. Completing it does not determine that any wages described here are in fact owed, and does not determine the outcome of any wage claim. Only the Labor Commissioner, or a court on appeal from the Labor Commissioner's decision, can determine whether wages are owed in a specific case.

THE LABOR COMMISSIONER'S AUTHORITY TO INVESTIGATE A WAGE CLAIM AND HOLD A HEARING
California law authorizes the Labor Commissioner to investigate employee complaints and to hold a hearing to recover wages, penalties, and other demands for compensation properly before the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, including claims for liquidated damages where the complaint alleges a wage below the applicable minimum wage. After a wage claim is filed, the Labor Commissioner has 30 days to notify the parties whether a hearing will be held, whether the matter will instead proceed under a separate statutory referral procedure (Labor Code section 98.3), or whether no further action will be taken on the complaint; if a hearing is set, it is generally required to be held within 90 days of that determination, subject to the Labor Commissioner's authority to allow more time where doing so would lead to an equitable and just resolution of the dispute. The Legislature has stated that hearings held under this statute are intended to be conducted in an informal setting that preserves the rights of the parties. A hearing of this kind is commonly referred to, outside the statute itself, as a "Berman hearing."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The Labor Commissioner is authorized to investigate employee complaints. The Labor Commissioner may provide for a hearing in any action to recover wages, penalties, and other demands for compensation, including liquidated damages if the complaint alleges payment of a wage less than the minimum wage fixed by an order of the Industrial Welfare Commission or by statute, properly before the division or the Labor Commissioner, including orders of the Industrial Welfare Commission, and shall determine all matters arising under his or her jurisdiction."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 98(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.)
  "Within 30 days of the filing of the complaint, the Labor Commissioner shall notify the parties as to whether a hearing will be held, whether action will be taken in accordance with Section 98.3, or whether no further action will be taken on the complaint. If the determination is made by the Labor Commissioner to hold a hearing, the hearing shall be held within 90 days of the date of that determination."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 98(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.)
  "It is the intent of the Legislature that hearings held pursuant to this section be conducted in an informal setting preserving the rights of the parties."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 98(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.)

All three citations below are to the same statutory subsection — Labor Code section 98(a) — quoted in different places for different points; that is disclosed here rather than presented as independent corroborating sources. The statute does not itself use the term "Berman hearing"; that is a commonly used name for this hearing process (after the legislator who authored the 1976 bill creating it) rather than statutory language, and this document does not independently verify the origin of that name beyond noting it is not part of the codified text quoted here. The statute also does not state, in the text quoted below, that a party at this kind of hearing does not need an attorney; the "informal setting" language is the closest statutory statement on that point, and any broader characterization of these hearings as not requiring legal representation is Labor Commissioner practice and public-facing agency guidance rather than statutory text verified in this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself file a wage claim with the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, does not determine that any specific wages are owed, and does not determine the outcome of any specific claim.

NOTICE OF THE HEARING AND THE EMPLOYER'S OPPORTUNITY TO ANSWER
When a hearing is set on a wage claim, California law requires that a copy of the complaint — including the amount of compensation requested — together with notice of the hearing's time and place, be served on all parties, either personally, by certified mail, or by a specific method of substituted service set out in the Code of Civil Procedure. After being served with that notice and complaint, a defendant employer has 10 days to file a written answer with the Labor Commissioner, in whatever form the Labor Commissioner prescribes, setting out the particulars in which the complaint is inaccurate or incomplete and the facts the defendant intends to rely on.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]

  — Cal. Labor Code § 98(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.)
  "(c) Within 10 days after service of the notice and the complaint, a defendant may file an answer with the Labor Commissioner in any form as the Labor Commissioner may prescribe, setting forth the particulars in which the complaint is inaccurate or incomplete and the facts upon which the defendant intends to rely."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 98(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.)

The two citations below are to different subsections of the same statutory section — Labor Code section 98, subdivisions (b) and (c) — which is disclosed here rather than presented as independent corroborating sources. THE LABOR COMMISSIONER'S ORDER, DECISION, OR AWARD (ODA)
Within 15 days after a Berman hearing concludes, the Labor Commissioner must file a copy of the order, decision, or award — commonly abbreviated ODA — with the division. The ODA must include a summary of the hearing and the reasons for the decision, and the Labor Commissioner must serve a copy on the parties personally, by first-class mail, or by the same substituted-service method used for the original notice. That service must also advise the parties of their right to appeal, and that failing to appeal within the prescribed period will make the ODA final and enforceable as a judgment of the superior court. For purposes of this chapter, an ODA includes any sums found owing, any damages proved, and any statutory penalties awarded. Amounts awarded for unpaid wages under an ODA accrue interest at the same rate that applies to prejudgment interest generally, running from the date the wages were originally due.

  — Cal. Labor Code § 98.1(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.1.)
  "The notice shall also advise the parties of their right to appeal the decision or award and further advise the parties that failure to do so within the period prescribed by this chapter shall result in the decision or award becoming final and enforceable as a judgment by the superior court."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 98.1(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.1.)
  "(b) For the purpose of this section, an award shall include any sums found owing, damages proved, and any penalties awarded pursuant to this code."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 98.1(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.1.)
  "(c) All awards granted pursuant to a hearing under this chapter shall accrue interest on all due and unpaid wages at the same rate as prescribed by subdivision (b) of Section 3289 of the Civil Code."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 98.1(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.1.)

APPEALING THE ODA TO SUPERIOR COURT: THE 10-DAY DEADLINE, TRIAL DE NOVO, AND THE EMPLOYER'S BOND
A party dissatisfied with the Labor Commissioner's order, decision, or award may appeal it to the superior court within 10 days after service of notice of the ODA. On appeal, the matter is heard "de novo" — meaning the superior court hears and decides the case anew, rather than reviewing the Labor Commissioner's decision for error. The party seeking review must pay a first-paper filing fee and serve a copy of the appeal on the Labor Commissioner. If the party appealing is the employer, California law imposes an additional condition on that appeal: before the appeal can proceed, the employer must post an undertaking — either a bond issued by a licensed surety or a cash deposit with the court — in the amount of the underlying order, decision, or award. That undertaking is conditioned on the employer paying any judgment later entered in the employee's favor, or the amount of the original ODA if the appeal is withdrawn or dismissed without a judgment (absent a settlement for a different amount). If the employer does not pay what it owes within 10 days after judgment, dismissal, withdrawal, or settlement, the undertaking — up to the full amount owed — is forfeited to the employee. The statute's undertaking requirement is directed, by its own terms, at an employer who appeals; it does not itself impose an equivalent bond-or-deposit condition on an employee who appeals.

FEE-SHIFTING ON AN UNSUCCESSFUL APPEAL OF THE ODA
If the party who appeals the Labor Commissioner's order, decision, or award to superior court is unsuccessful in that appeal, California law requires the court to determine the costs and reasonable attorney's fees incurred by the other parties to the appeal, and to assess that amount against the party who filed the appeal. By its terms, this rule applies to whichever party files the appeal — employer or employee — and loses, not to one side only; the statute separately specifies that, where the employee is the party defending against an appeal, the employee is considered "successful" if the court awards any amount greater than zero.

An employee is successful if the court awards an amount greater than zero."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 98.2(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.2.)

FINALITY OF THE ODA AND ENTRY OF JUDGMENT WHEN NO APPEAL IS FILED
If no party files a notice of appeal from the Labor Commissioner's order, decision, or award within the statutory 10-day period, California law provides that the ODA becomes the final order, in the absence of fraud. Once the order is final, the Labor Commissioner must file a certified copy of it with the clerk of the superior court, and the clerk enters judgment on it immediately, unless the parties have reached a settlement approved by the Labor Commissioner. A judgment entered this way has the same force and effect, and is subject to the same rules, as any other civil judgment, and it may be enforced the same way — with the statute directing that enforcement of the judgment receive court priority.

FILING DEADLINES THAT MAY APPLY TO AN UNDERLYING WAGE CLAIM
Neither the statute establishing DLSE wage-claim hearings nor the Labor Commissioner's implementing procedures addressed elsewhere in this document set out a single, fixed number of years within which a wage claim must be filed. California's general civil statutes of limitations set different filing deadlines depending on how a claim for unpaid compensation is legally characterized: an action on a liability created by statute, other than a penalty or forfeiture, must generally be brought within three years; an action on a contract, obligation, or liability not founded on a written instrument must generally be brought within two years; and an action on a contract, obligation, or liability founded on a written instrument must generally be brought within four years.

That undertaking is conditioned on the employer paying any judgment later entered in the employee's favor, or the amount of the original ODA if the appeal is withdrawn or dismissed without a judgment (absent a settlement for a different amount). If the employer does not pay what it owes within 10 days after judgment, dismissal, withdrawal, or settlement, the undertaking — up to the full amount owed — is forfeited to the employee. The statute's undertaking requirement is directed, by its own terms, at an employer who appeals; it does not itself impose an equivalent bond-or-deposit condition on an employee who appeals.

expectedJSON.body: If no party files a notice of appeal from the Labor Commissioner's order, decision, or award within the statutory 10-day period, California law provides that the ODA becomes the final order, in the absence of fraud. Once the order is final, the Labor Commissioner must file a certified copy of it with the clerk of the superior court, and the clerk enters judgment on it immediately, unless the parties have reached a settlement approved by the Labor Commissioner. A judgment entered this way has the same force and effect, and is subject to the same rules, as any other civil judgment, and it may be enforced the same way — with the statute directing that enforcement of the judgment receive court priority.

California's general civil statutes of limitations set different filing deadlines depending on how a claim for unpaid compensation is legally characterized: an action on a liability created by statute, other than a penalty or forfeiture, must generally be brought within three years; an action on a contract, obligation, or liability not founded on a written instrument must generally be brought within two years; and an action on a contract, obligation, or liability founded on a written instrument must generally be brought within four years.
